title: IBM Connect to Cloud Design Leadership
summary: Led design for IBM Connect to Cloud, a hybrid cloud initiative connecting on-premise IBM software to the cloud through registration, usage, and cognitive advisory services. Built and directed a distributed team across multiple years and many releases, and represented design in customer engagements and executive playbacks.

children.text: I was the design lead for IBM Connect to Cloud, a hybrid cloud initiative connecting on-premise IBM software to the cloud through registration, usage, and cognitive advisory services. Across multiple years and many releases, I led a growing design team and represented design in customer engagements and executive playbacks.
The work was about organizing a team around a gap in the market, articulating the problem, and operationalizing design to solve it.

Customers had no clear picture of the IBM software running across their data centers, and IBM didn't have one either, which made it hard to know what to charge them. Connect to Cloud closed that gap: it registered on-premise inventory to IBM Cloud and surfaced it through a coherent set of services, with cognitive advisory recommendations on top.

blocks.alt: Connect to Cloud registration page, abstracted. A form for naming an environment, entering an endpoint and credentials, and tagging the registration — IBM brand stripped, generic chrome.
blocks.caption: The registration entry point — how on-premise inventory got into IBM Cloud.

blocks.text: I led design from the initial whiteboarding to the eventual release and customer impact.

children.text: Two personas defined the work. Andy, an IT administrator running data centers full of IBM software with no clear inventory of what was where. Anne, a capacity planner trying to right-size workloads, plan upgrades, and spot waste. Both had been guessing with spreadsheets for years.
Our design strategy moved the product up a maturity ladder, one stage at a time.

items.body: Give customers an inventory so they could finally see what IBM software they had.
Surface usage on top, so they could spot waste and right-size before it grew.
Forecast anomalies and patterns from the usage data.
Cognitive advisory recommendations that told customers what to do next.

blocks.alt: Two persona cards side by side. Left card: Andy, IT administrator, with notes on managing data centers full of IBM software and no clear inventory. Right card: Anne, capacity planner, with notes on right-sizing workloads, planning upgrades, and spotting waste — both guessing with spreadsheets.
blocks.caption: Andy and Anne — the two users the product was built around.

children.text: I led a team of seven designers and a researcher, distributed from Austin to the UK. Beyond the product features themselves, the team built design-ops infrastructure that contributed to future IBM Design patterns across the company. We created a Sketch nested-symbols system that eliminated redlining for engineering, established weekly design-share critiques, and focused on the content layer by creating documentation as we went (something design hadn't been a part of at IBM yet).
I directed the team and designed alongside them through the many releases.

blocks.alt: Schematic of a Sketch nested-symbols system. A parent symbol contains nested child symbols labelled with state variants, arrows showing overrides cascading from parent to child, and a small key labelled 'no more redlining'.
blocks.caption: The Sketch nested-symbols pattern the team built — a design-ops contribution that outlived the product.

sections.title: Working with customers and senior stakeholders

children.text: We relied on real customers to get accurate insights: the Sponsor User Program, workshops with global partners, and conference roundtables. A researcher backed the work with usability tests, ethnographies, and heuristic reviews.
I played design back to the Design Executives every two weeks, and during VP reviews I defended our design direction and choices.

The product shipped GA on Bluemix in the first year. The platform migrated to IBM Cloud Marketplace in the second. By the end, the work had jumpstarted three core capabilities inside IBM Cloud Private, the platform that anchored IBM's hybrid cloud strategy.
The role was my first time leading designers and my first time sitting in executive playbacks. Both became a huge part of my career.
The cognitive advisory work was the first of many AI chat advisors I designed. A pattern that has become ubiquitous a decade later.

blocks.alt: Horizontal timeline of three ship milestones. Year one: GA on Bluemix. Year two: migration to IBM Cloud Marketplace. End of program: jumpstarted three core capabilities of IBM Cloud Private — Software Metering, Catalog, and Transformation Advisor.
blocks.caption: The ship arc — Bluemix, Marketplace, then the trio of capabilities that landed in IBM Cloud Private.
